utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, assisted by Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning. Eugene O'Sullivan, Tatjana Savic, and Deirdre Montgomery for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing that need delay us, we would have the usher escort the witness to the stand. While he is coming in, I would indicate to counsel that because of a commitment that the Judges have, we are slightly varying the schedule today so that with we will sit in two 100-minute sessions with a half-hour break in between. So 9.00 to 10.40; and then 11.10 and 12.50 and rise for the day at that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. Good morning to you, sir. Would you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. My name is Radomir Njegus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth and what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on 24th of June, 1956, in Foca. I'm a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you testified previously before the Tribunal or at any of the courts in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not before this Tribunal, but I did testify before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the trial against Gojko Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. In this Tribunal, which you would be aware, is created for the specific purpose of dealing with certain crimes in the former Yugoslavia. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and the procedure here is not very much different from the procedures with which you would be familiar from your experience as a lawyer or in trials in which you would have participated previously. Here the side calling you - in this case, as I said, the Prosecution - would begin, after which, the -- counsel for each of the accused would have an opportunity to cross-examine you. And the -- when you're -- following any re-examination that the side calling you may have, the Bench may have some questions of you. Now, it has been indicated to us that the Prosecution would wish to examine you for three hours, and counsel for the accused Stanisic for six hours, followed by counsel for the accused Zupljanin for an hour and a half. Ordinarily, for technical reasons having to do with the recording system which the Tribunal has, the Tribunal sits for periods of not longer than 90 minutes. And there's a break, and -- and then we resume. If it's a morning session, the trial day would begin at 9.00 and end at 1.45. If it's an afternoon session, which tomorrow is, the trial day would begin at 2.15 an end at 7.00. Today is a little unusual in that the sessions set would be a little longer. They will not exceed 100 minutes, but they may be as long as that for reasons of which counsel would be aware. So today, and today alone, we will sit for an hour and 40 minutes, then have a half-hour break, and then have another session of an hour and 40 minutes. Of course, notwithstanding the -- those time indications, if, for any reason you need a break, if you indicate it to us then, of course, we would accommodate you. Before I invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin the examination-in-chief, is there anything that you would wish to raise? There is one -- one further thing, that you would have begun by making the solemn declaration and, again, as a lawyer, I probably needn't remind you of this, but I must for the record point that the Tribunal is empowered to deal with incidents of untruthful evidence, so the pain of the penalty of perjury attends witnesses before this Tribunal. So is there any query that you have that I might seek to answer before counsel begins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any questions. Everything is clear. I was treated fairly by the people to the right of me. I would just like to say hello to my former colleagues, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin. We have changed a locality physically, we haven't seen each other for a long time, but I just wanted to say hello to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to begin by just outlining for the purposes of the Court how you come to be giving evidence. First of all, I think you were seen originally by members of the Office of the Prosecutor in February of 2003; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If that's what it can be called, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to deal with this quite shortly. They came to speak to you. I don't think that at the time you appreciated fully that it was an interview. And you were neither given any rights nor, indeed, were you ever shown any record of that interview until you arrived at the Tribunal yesterday. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, in 2007, in September, were you interviewed again by the Office of the Prosecutor; this time the proceedings were tape-recorded; and you were told that you were being interviewed as a witness? And you were given, I think, earlier in this year, in May, a copy of the transcript of that interview, which you had an opportunity to read through. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And having read it through, are you satisfied that it's accurately recorded what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked if you wanted to make any changes, is this right, and you said, No, with the exception of adding something in respect of a gentleman - if that's the right word - called Batko who was operating in the Grbavica area during 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who has very recently been arrested. And you were anxious to make it clear that Mico Stanisic, as far as you were concerned, had ordered the arrest of Batko in 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, otherwise, you did not wish to make any changes to what you said in the interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Nothing material. I made a comment then, saying that I was not specific in several instances, but today we will have an opportunity to clear this up. But as far as any actual changes or corrections, no, I haven't noticed anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can I briefly deal with your career. Effectively, for most of your working life, have you been a professional policeman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You graduated in 1974 from the police academy. You originally started work in Foca, which, as you say, is where you were born. And then in 1977 did you move to the Sarajevo SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You graduated in the earlier 1980s from law school. And then did you have a -- a break for about two years, between 1988 and 1990? Did you work for the municipality of Sarajevo? In other words, you left the police for a couple of years?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's right. About two years and -- about four years and a few days. And, at the time, I worked for the party structures of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that next. Were you, in fact, a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not only was I a member of the League of Communists, I also was employed as the executive secretary of the presidency of the committee of the League of Communists in the municipality of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In 1990, however, did you go back to the Sarajevo SUP, and were you the chief of uniformed police until 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. I became the chief of uniformed police, as you called it, for the whole city of Sarajevo, in the city SUP, as it was called. So I was head of the uniformed police for the entire city of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you then -- did you then lose your job after the 1990 elections and the division of posts between the three nationalist parties within the -- the BiH MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. After the takeover of power by the national parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a consequence of all the events was that about after one year or so of performing the duties of head or chief of uniformed police I lost my job. I was relieved from post by a policeman who was trained as a butcher. For -- I didn't have any engagement in the police after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you receive any kind of support from the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, after the split that took place in the MUP, when the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed, did you receive a position in the Serbian MUP in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, then. But, if you allow me, we've skipped one period of time. After I was relieved of duty from that previous position, after having spent two months without any police engagements, I was assigned to a different post. I was assigned to a post of a republic police inspector in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP, starting on 3rd of June in 1991. And I spent some time at that post. And only after that, we have this, what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right, sir. I'm so sorry. I skipped that one post. Now, we'll look at your appointment in a moment. But can we just, first of all, have a look at a chart that's been prepared of the -- the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's P -- let me just get this right. P876. I think it might be -- yes. Let's turn it round.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do we see there that you were appointed, if we look at line number 9, we can focus to the right-hand side of the ... Can we see there that your position was that of -- of assistant minister --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the administration for legal, personnel, and administrative tasks, you were the assistant minister for legal, personnel, and alien affairs. We see your name under that of Mr. Radovic. Can you explain the division of responsibility of posts between you and Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. With the start of the operation and organisation of MUP, Republika Srpska MUP, on 4th of April, 1992, my position was more of a formal nature of position of the head of the cabinet of the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska. The first minister, of course, was Mr. Mico Stanisic. That was my first formal appointment. I was chief of his cabinet. I have a decision appointing me in my possession. Since I was at that position for no more than about a month. After about a month, I got the position of the acting chief of administration for legal, personnel, and alien affairs, as you told, Ms. Prosecutor. So from the 4th of April, 1992, Mr. Nenad Radovic was in charge or was appointed chief of the administration for personnel administrative tasks. And about a month later I took over from him, and I remained on that position until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just then now have a look, please, at the later decision which is at tab 25, which, for some reason, wasn't on our 65 ter list. But I don't think it matters much since I'm not going to ask for it to be exhibited. It's 10370.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That shows that in a decision of the 15th of May, Mico Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we pull up the bottom, please, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- appoints you as head of office of the ministry secretary in the staff of the MUP, and this -- it says, Of which the staff for commanding and controlling of force of the ministry shall be formed. Can you tell us what that decision is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend Ms. Korner. We need a clarification here. Actually, Ms. Korner mentioned at -- it's page 9, line 7, that decision was issued on 15th of May. But the wording here is not confirming that. Actually, in the preamble, it's a decision, previous decision, of Mico Stanisic, but we don't know -- maybe sometimes later it was this particular decision. But can you clarify, please, with the witness, if he knows, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Njegus, I said the 15th of May, and Mr. Pantelic rightly points out that it says, According to an order of the 15th of May, as opposed to being appointed on the 15th of May. Are you able to tell us when this decision -- when you received this appointment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot remember precisely. Probably I received this decision on or about the 15th of May. If I may, I'll try to explain briefly the situation about the alleged staff, if this is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In my earlier statements given to the investigators of the OTP, I also explained the situation about the alleged functioning and establishment of a so-called staff of the MUP units and so on. In fact, I confirmed in the same way as I wish to confirm now that it was, in fact, a fictitious staff that was only allegedly established, but it never really got off the ground in any way, operationally or administratively. The adoption of such a decision, not only this one mentioning my name but other decisions too, was preceded by other decisions or something of the kind. That document is in existence. I had the opportunity to read it. And that document states some tasks of the staff I mentioned. Whether or not it was necessary to establish it, I don't know. Probably yes. But that staff, as envisaged, has never been either established, nor did it start functioning. This decision that I also received after another decision signed by the minister was nothing but a piece of paper. It didn't contain anything new with regard to my position. It only referred to some of my work-related duties. This is what I wanted to say about this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now one other thing, because we're going to deal with that in a moment, this is apparently signed by Mico Stanisic. Can you tell us anything about the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is, indeed, the signature of Mr. Mico Stanisic. But this isn't his authentic signature. I mean that this decision and many other documents were supposed to be signed by him personally. This is, actually, an authenticated copy which -- which was authenticated by a facsimile, as many other documents. Any doctor, a specialist or a general practitioner, may have a stamp with a facsimile replacing their signature. So this decision and other similar documents were also authenticated by the facsimile. The facsimile was not in the possession of Mr. Stanisic, but, as far as I know, Mr. Radovic had it. So he authenticated most documents, including such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did anybody other than Mr. Radovic have this facsimile signature of Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That was possible. I cannot be sure. He may not have the facsimile stamp on him all the time. It was probably in an office or several offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there -- to your knowledge, was there one stamp, one facsimile, as it were, of his signature or more than one?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I personally think that there was only one. But, as I said, it's possible that it was in the same place, the stamp of the MUP of Republika Srpska was. Again, I think, personally, that there was only one such facsimile stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever have position -- position -- possession of it, in order to sign documents on behalf of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's why I gave a tentative answer a minute ago with regard to the logical situation that the facsimile was kept together with the other stamps and seals. With regard to that, yes, it was probably possible to me to have access to -- to them and authenticate or certify something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are there documents that you authenticated with the facsimile signature of Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't think so because there was no need for me to do so. As far as I remember, I didn't. But I could have if I had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What exactly -- well, actually perhaps we'll finish on this document. You say this document was fictitious; there was no such staff that existed. Do you know why, therefore, this decision was made or this document was produced?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, the document isn't fictitious. The document was undoubtedly issued. I cannot remember precisely; it was 18 years ago. Probably at the beginning of the war, or the war was just starting, the decision was taken to establish such a staff. But this is merely a logical conclusion. It's another question why it never started functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sorry. I just need to go back to what you actually said. Yes. All right. What you said was this was: "... a fictitious staff that was only allegedly established, but it never really got off the ground in any way operationally or administratively." I suppose the real question then should be: Why was there a document -- not the document being fictitious but that related to what you describe as a fictitious staff? Why was that document produced?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I wasn't the one who took the decision about its establishment. But as a man who lived in those times and as a professional, I am trying to -- I'll try to give it a thought. The war was starting, and the MUP had its so-called peacetime establishment and structure which was at the basis of its work. But, on the other hand, there was this -- the other reality, namely, the war that had started. Wouldn't it be normal to adapt the structure to the new circumstances on the ground? That's my conclusion. And, as far as I remember, that was the reason behind the decision to establish such a staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why -- do you know why nothing ever happened, in reality? Why there never was a staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't know. As you see, I was supposed to be some sort of secretary here. That is a -- that was a technical position in the framework of such a staff. But there has -- hasn't been one meeting of that staff, not one session, literally. Why, I cannot say. But probably because the one who was officially the head of that staff never called such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was officially the head of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the then-minister, Mr. Stanisic. As far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not on our 65 ter list but there's been quite a lot of evidence about it and the effect of the facsimile signature is something that's going to come up. If there is an objection, then I won't pursue it; but otherwise, I would quite like to make it an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Counsel, we are not unappreciative of the possible relevance of this document, but we must state for the record that we are not happy, for want of a better word, of the manner in which it is coming in. So -- but for purely practical purposes, for purely practical reasons, we take the exceptional course of allowing it to be admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Exhibit P1407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you move on, if that was your intention --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would like stay just a little while with this document. Because I would like to ask the witness, Mr. Njegus, if you could explain to us, then, what happened instead. Because I'm sure that, somehow, the minister, Mr. Stanisic, was assisted by some staff. And if it wasn't this staff, then who else, then, came to the assistance of Mr. Stanisic? Was there, so to say, a shadow cabinet that functioned instead of the one that you had described but which never came into force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure that I understood your question properly. I don't think that there was a shadow cabinet. I can say that for a fact. I can also say for a fact that Mr. Stanisic obviously relied on his associates and his closest associates from that period; we know who they were. Under-secretaries for public and state security. And they, in their turn, relied on chiefs of administration, primarily on the chiefs of operative administrations. According to what I know, there was no shadow cabinet. There were a few people who performed their duties responsibly. And Mr. Stanisic, as minister, of course, could rely on those people, and he did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But were the people in the minister's cabinet actually appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so your testimony is that it was just because of the fact that the head of the staff never convened the persons who had been pointed and that was the reason why it never became effective. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a second, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Madam Korner, let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before -- sorry, just before we do move on, just so we're absolutely clear about this document, it says you were to be appointed as head of office to the minister strictly in the staff to command and control the overall forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So whether or not it existed, was it intended to be a -- a sort of cabinet to advise the minister in respect of his deployment of MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not only were they supposed to advise and help the minister but also take decisions. That's how I saw the purpose of that staff, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you mentioned in answer to His Honour Judge Harhoff's question that he relied on his closest -- sorry, I just have to go back again and just get your right words. Here. Yes. "... Mr. Stanisic obviously relied on his associates and his closest associates from that period; we know who they were." Who were Mr. Stanisic's closest associates during this period around May of 1992 and until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Whether we wanted or not, it was not just on paper. That's how things were. His closest associates were under-secretaries for state and public security which was only logical. Mr. Slobodan Skipina in charge of state security, and, later, he was replaced by Dragan Kijac, if I'm not mistaken. And as far as public security was concerned, the under-secretary was Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. What about Mr. Karisik, who, if we look at the plan - I'm not going to ask for it to be turned up again - was the head of the special police detachment. How close was he to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't know how close he was to him. The private things never were of much interest to see. However, Mr. Karisik who was the commander of the 1st Special Unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska and later on the commander of the detachment of Republika Srpska, which was rather numerous, played a very significant role as the commander of that unit throughout the war or, rather, up to the period during which he discharged those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kovac, Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Tomo Kovac was also one of important people throughout the existence of the MUP of Republika Srpska. From the beginning of April 1992, he was chief of the public security station in Ilidza. And then a month or a month and a half later he became chief of the administration of uniformed police. It was a very important administration at the time. All uniformed police officers were members of that administration, both active and reserve police officers. Tomo Kovac was their superior. And in that position, obviously, he was a very important person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what technically did your responsibilities as the assistant minister for personnel and legal affairs -- what technically did that -- were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: As far as my part of responsibilities and obligations went, I was, just like everybody else, acting chief, because we had never been appointed to our positions formally, and we should have been appointed by the government of Republika Srpska. But that's just the formal side of the things. As far as my obligations and responsibilities were concerned, you have to bear in mind that all those things were happening at the beginning of the war when all the institutions were created from scratch. One of them being the MUP of Republika Srpska. I started working first on my own and then I was joined by two or three or five to six associates before the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can -- can I stop you. We don't have that much time. Can I -- can you just tell me what your job responsibilities were, in theory at least.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Partly theoretically and partly in fact what we did was as follows: Drafting regulations for Republika Srpska within the scope of Internal Affairs. We were involved in several such legislative projects. We also monitored and analysed the personnel in the entire MUP of Republika Srpska. And we also had certain authorities with regard to foreign nationals. But in objective terms, we spent the least time on that last task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did your job involve you in making appointments within the ministry? And by "within the ministry," I mean the whole ministry.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No, not really. I would normally be informed about any such meeting, just like anybody else, and then I would prepare the material for the upcoming meeting within my scope of work, as far as that was possible. I would prepare to talk about things from my scope of duties, if I was called to join the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think there have been a mistranslation somewhere, because what I actually asked you was whether your job responsibility included making personnel appointments within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If we're talking about the first month or so, when I was considered chef de cabinet, then, yes, that would have been part of my duties. But there were no such meetings in factual terms. And if we're taking about at a later period, then those things would not be arranged through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So -- sorry. In order for personnel to be appointed - is that what you're saying? - there would have to be a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, madam. What's the link between meetings and appointments?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm asking, and that's why I'm wondering about what's going on in the translation. If you were appointing -- sorry. If people were to be appointed to positions either within the ministry itself, the headquarters, or elsewhere, would that be part of your responsibility to make or to recommend appointments?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Now I understand you fully. No, that was not part of our competences and authorities. Our service, the one that I was in charge of, was very small. It grew a bit later. We were just a technical staff. And if somebody was appointed, then we would just do the technical part of that job. In other words, we were not in charge of proposing anything, or -- it -- unless the appointments concerned personnel and my own office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you mean personnel within your own office? Or personnel generally?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean my own administration, as it were. And there were very few of us. Later on, after a year or two or maybe even after three years, I was consulted about all appointments within the service that I was in charge of, even in the territories of Security Services Centres, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "later on," when was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: As the conditions of work started becoming a bit more normal, in 1993, 1994, or even 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you report directly to Mico Stanisic, or to either Mr. Kljajic or Mr. Skipina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Under the law, I was directly answerable to Mr. Stanisic. But I have to be very honest and admit that, in factual terms, on a daily basis, I had much more communication with Kljajic, who had just recently been appointed, and some others. And when it came to my day-to-day job, I had much more contacts with other people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you yourself have -- take any part in the activities which led to the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You saw some minutes of a meeting that took place on February the 11th in Banja Luka. Your name does not appear. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No. I perhaps would attend them, but I was never called. I was never informed about any meetings, and I never attended any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, next, I want to move on to your knowledge of Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. First, Mico Stanisic. By 1992, how long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not long. But I would say long enough. Mr. Stanisic and I attended the same school, the secondary police school in Vrace, the place often mentioned. He was the first generation that graduated, and I was the second generation. And I already said that I have no reason to hide anything. I was not Mico Stanisic's trusted person. However, Mico Stanisic, whom I knew at school, was an excellent student, a good athlete, and a good person. While he was in charge of the Republika Srpska MUP and when it comes to the pre-war period when he was the secretary of the Sarajevo city SUP, I have already stated, and I'm repeating that statement because there's nothing to hide, he was a professional. He had a lot of professional qualities. And whatever he did, he did it conscientiously. He was a hard-working person who demanded a lot from those that he worked with, and that made him a bit difficult for cooperation. He demanded discipline, he demanded order. But as a -- as head, he was very specific. I have already spoken about that. He drew maximum from everybody, from everybody he worked with, but he also knew how to delegate responsibilities and obligations to them. And that's how things functioned. That would be my perception of Mico Stanisic as a -- a head of -- a head of service and a member of that same service. And we -- with your permission, I would just like to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, no. I'm going to come to Mr. Zupljanin. I'd like to finish with Mr. Stanisic, please. You say that you -- you were not Mico Stanisic's trusted person. Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I can make some estimates on personal level. One on the principle level or on the -- as a matter of principle was the fact that I was a member of the League of Communists, which, at certain later stages, was not a very good thing to have been. Mico Stanisic, I'm not sure whether he was or was not member of the SDS, but he was somebody from that area. So that was one of the major reasons why I couldn't have been his most trusted person or trusted person. There may have been other personal reasons, but I don't know whether they are of any importance here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say: I don't know whether he was a member or not a member of the SDS, but he was a someone from that area. What area? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's what I meant. Had he not been somebody SDS can accept, he wouldn't have been the Ministry of Interior. That should suffice. Now, how close his affiliation was, whether he was in or not, whether it was formal or not; I don't have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say one of the major reasons was you were a member of the League of Communists and not of the SDS, and then you said there may have been other personal reasons. What sort of reasons?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I was thinking about it, and I was thinking about these things because that's my approach to life. I try to do things thoroughly. So I thought about it, and since it happened that at the time Mr. Mico Stanisic, in late 1993, if I'm not mistaken, was again appointed Ministry of the Interior, I was the first, maybe the only one, among the people in the senior structures of the Republika Srpska MUP who was relieved of duty. I was wondering why. Apparently I was not irresponsible in carrying out my duties, so I thought over it and my conclusion was that it may have had to do with a misunderstanding related to formal disbanding of the units of so-called Malovic unit. Because at that time, I, in my function of the chief of personnel, and so on, affairs, issued an order for them to be relieved of duty as members of MUP because this unit hadn't been doing anything for a longer period. But I was ordered to do so by Tomo Kovac. I still remember the telephone conversation well. Later on, I was indirectly told that Mr. Stanisic took it against me. It may be that he's hearing this for the first time, namely, that it wasn't something I did on my own initiative, that instead I was ordered to do so by Mr. Kovac. And I cannot remember and I don't think it's important what his position was at the time, but there may be another -- but -- reason but that reason is probably trivial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to look at a document in relation to Mr. Malovic's unit in a moment. But your understanding was that Mr. Stanisic has objected to your disbanding Malovic's unit which was then still being paid as a MUP unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's only my conclusion. Maybe it's not a true state of affairs; it's just the way I see things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you -- let's move, then, to Mr. Zupljanin next. When did you first come across him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It's hard to say specifically when. I do know of Mr. Zupljanin, of course. I had known about him even before the war, before 1992. Both of us were at certain positions within the police. I do know of him since back then. I know that he was a successful chief of the security centre in Banja Luka. I know that he was one of the people who, all of us, in the MUP of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was viewed as a gentleman, a person liberal-minded. And I cannot remember when was it that we met for the first time, but I am sure that we were together at the collegium that was held in Belgrade, the first such collegium. Later on I have seen him at many meetings, both working meetings and other meetings. And I would like to add that my personal view of him is a positive one, both in personal terms and in terms of professional cooperation. He has had a problem of his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Vladimir Tutus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come on to Mr. Tutus in a moment. But when you were first interviewed, you told the investigators that you thought that he was the deputy of Minister Stanisic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's right. I believed that Mr. Zupljanin, in addition to his position of the chief of the CSB Banja Luka, was also deputy of the minister of the interior. That's how I saw him throughout. And only recently, after having had conversations with some of my colleagues, colleagues who should have known about such things, I realised they convinced me that I wasn't right in my beliefs. They asked me, Where did you come to that conclusion and how? But that's what I believed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and obviously I'm going to ask you exactly what your colleagues asked you is, What you gave you the impression --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, Ms. Korner, but it is not recorded, the last sentence, the last words that Mr. Njegus said after the words: "But" -- it's line 17. "But that's what I believed." And it's quite important, I mean, what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I interrupted because I thought had you finished. You told us that your colleagues asked how you had come to the conclusion and how [sic]. And you added "... that's what I believed." And did you say something else? Mr. Pantelic thinks you said something else.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he's right. I said that obviously I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You obviously were wrong, and I accept that. But what I want to ask you is the same thing that your colleagues asked you. What led you to believe that he was in such a high position that he was deputy minister to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer. I tried to explain that I just believed so. I don't know what the basis for my belief was. I was even convinced that he received a decision appointing him to that position. I -- I really cannot explain why was it that I believed such a thing, but I was wrong. I apologise if I have misled anyone because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But -- but, clearly, there must have been something either about his behaviour or his interaction with Mico Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There must have been something that led you to believe that, whether it was in his behaviour or his interaction with Mico Stanisic. Can you try and put your finger on what it was that led you to believe that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to tread there. I simply - me, personally - believed that he was even formally appointed to that position. I never tried to verify that until recently. And a few days ago I was told that I was wrong, and it seems I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But -- I'm sorry to press you on this, but it's really quite important, Mr. Njegus. What was it that gave you the impression that Stojan Zupljanin, chief of the CSB in Banja Luka, actually held a high position as deputy minister to Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I must repeat a sentence I uttered just recently. It's because I believed that was formally appointed to the -- to this position. And since I believed that, I then believed that he actually was deputy minister. And since my first belief was wrong, then everything stemming from it was also wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you saw him - for example, at the 11th of July meeting in Belgrade - did his -- his speeches or his attitude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I appreciate that your persistence suggests that this is a matter that you consider important. But having regard to the answers that the witness has consistently given, isn't this a matter that you must let go and move on? People come to erroneous conclusions for any number of reasons which they are not necessarily able to explain either at the time or later on. And the witness has -- has answered, as I understand it as best he could, on at least three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I think it is quite important, given the nature of this case, as to why this witness should have formed this impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic's objection about your leading him, which I didn't respond to a short while ago, the -- the way your question -- the direction of your recent questions are pressing him for conclusions which I don't know is necessarily helpful to us at the end of the day. As I said, I appreciate that your -- you regard the issue as important, but perhaps you need to try a different tact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried about three different tacts. And, Your Honour, I may say, I'm a little surprised to hear that given what we say is the case as against these two men, that Your Honour shouldn't find this an important matter. But I dealt with it for the moment, as far as I can. I take that on board, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. You were -- you mentioned that he had problems with Mr. Tutus. How did you come to be aware of those problems with Mr. Tutus?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I didn't have any problems with Tutus. The person who had problems with Tutus was Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I pause for a moment. There seems to be a real problem with translation this morning. I think it really is quite important that we try and get this across.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said there was a problem that Mr. Zupljanin had with Mr. Zupljanin -- with Zupljanin. I'm sorry. That Mr. Zupljanin had with Mr. Tutus. How did you come to learn of the problem?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I knew about that from the very beginning, from the moment the communication or connection with Banja Luka was established. Namely, in the city of Banja Luka, there was a public security station, having its chief, and that was the practice that applied to all the places which were seats of the CSBs, that the local public security stations had their chiefs. I must add that this practice later on turned to seem very impractical, including the issues related to Tutus, and therefore we abandoned such practice. Immediately after the communication was established, this Mr. Tutus, again a person who was first generation, who attended the high school for police affairs together with Mr. Stanisic, would call every once in a while, maybe three times a day, mostly to complain or I would even say snitch on Mr. Zupljanin in relation to very trivial issues occasionally. Because he himself was narcicisstic and very ambitious. He wanted to topple Mr. Zupljanin and take his place. All of us had problems with him for quite a long period of time, problems of that sort. In order to resolve the situation, in order to help Mr. Zupljanin, I remember that what we did was promote Mr. Tutus even to the position of the chief of the administration for uniformed police, and he spent several months with us in Bijeljina. That's how we tried to help Mr. Zupljanin get rid of his problems. I don't know whether we succeeded. But that was why I mentioned Mr. Tutus. Namely, his unprofessional approach to work was something that was making things difficult for Mr. Zupljanin, putting obstacles for him in his work. I don't know whether this is of any importance for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I really apologise again. It's line -- it's page 28, line 17, after the word "his problems," witness said, To get rid of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's not -- let's not tell him what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. "Posast." A word which means "the plague." So it's just a reference to the translation. Maybe you can ask him again. He doesn't hear, plague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Instead of "problems," the word should be "plague"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, because problems at the level of -- of his description of the level of the problem was like a plague. My understanding that Mr. Tutus was a plague for [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... all right, all right, all right, Mr. Pantelic. I've got the point. Perhaps the interpreters can help us. Is that the word that he used?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: The Serbian word "posast" means literally "epidemic," but it would be better interpreted into English maybe as "affliction" in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I just want to ask you whether you're able to recall. You say he was complaining about Mr. Zupljanin on trivial matters; can you recall what any of those matters about which Mr. Tutus was complaining?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If I could recall, I would probably have to speak about it for ten days because the man did it daily three times, to me any way. But there were about ten higher-ranking officers he would call and tell on Mr. Zupljanin. Those were mostly trivial things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Possibly some of these objections were founded. I -- I'm not saying that everything was unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, did anybody -- that's what I want to -- the final question on this. Did anybody actually go and speak to Mr. Zupljanin from MUP headquarters about the complaints that were making -- that Mr. Tutus was making to see if they had any justification?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I went to Banja Luka many times for several reasons. We tried to resolve the problem in various ways but to little avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this in 1992 or later?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Later. More likely later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What do you mean after 1992? In 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It is more likely that it was in 1993 when the conditions were more normal to -- with regard to the functioning of the MUP for us to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Zupljanin, for example at the 11th of July meeting in Belgrade, did you raise with him any of the complaints that Mr. Tutus had made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Logically, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Because in July 1992 -- the meeting took place on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade, if I'm not mistaken. So it was only a few months after the beginning of the new functioning. Communication with Banja Luka was only established in the autumn of 1992. At that time, there was that meeting in Belgrade. Tutus didn't matter at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, what I asked you was why you hadn't -- I'll start this one again. When you say there was no communication with Banja Luka until autumn 1992, do you really mean there was no communication at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I didn't say there was no communication at all. I meant telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once the corridor was opened by the end of June, wasn't there telephone and other types of police communication with Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Probably that -- that is not an issue. But I cannot place it precisely in time. June, July, August ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So just to finalise the matters on this particular subject, it was not until 1993 that you spoke to Mr. Zupljanin at all about the complaints that Mr. Tutus was making?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's what I said. I probably spoke to Mr. Zupljanin on several occasions in late 1992 and in 1993 and later. That's not an issue. If for no other reason than because of this man Tutus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are you now saying, sir, that you did, in 1992, speak to Mr. Zupljanin about the complaints, which you describe as trivial, that Mr. Tutus was making?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Zupljanin, at any stage, explain to you what it was that was causing Mr. Tutus to make these complaints?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No. I can't remember him explaining that to me, but it wasn't necessary either. Because it was a generally known fact that Mr. Tutus - and this is not only my opinion - was not a person with whom you could cooperate, that he was a problematic personality, a narcissistic man.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you said that already. All right. Now, to begin with, were you -- when you first began your job, were you stationed in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Depending which job. If you mean legal and personnel affairs, there were some conditions at Jahorina in the so-called Kosuta facility. I was able to work on some of these legislative projects with some co-workers. That was possible there. But only in the second half of July when we moved to Bijeljina, we did have -- well, I dare say, even good conditions for work, and only there did we start to carry out our duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. The actual question I asked you was: When you first began your job, were you -- as minister, assistant minister, were you stationed in Vrace school?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If you mean legal and personnel affairs and so on, yes. At Vrace, it was orally agreed that I should take over these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I explain to you, which I clearly have to, I'm just interested in the places in which you were based. Did you remain in Vrace until May?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then did you go to Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from Jahorina, did you move to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you moved from Jahorina to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It's difficult to be precise. Well, approximately in early July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to look -- ask you to look, please, at a number of appointments, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, first of all, 2363, 65 ter 2363.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This -- this and a whole lot of other discussions are all dated the 1st of April. Had you started work by the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If you mean me personally, no, not I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Looking at the stamp on that, are you able to say whether this is a real or a facsimile signature? Looking at the -- sorry, the signature of Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: This is, without any doubt, a facsimile stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know why, which we'll see, there were a whole lot of other temporary appointments of chiefs of CSBs? Why all these temporary appointments were made on the 1st of April? And I mean why the posts were temporary.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't know that. Because as I have already stated, neither on the 1st of April nor before that, I was immediately involved in these activities, so I cannot say. I can only make conclusions why all these decisions or these appointments are temporary. It does seem logical or natural to some extent, though, because at the time, as far as I know, there was -- there were no rules about the structure of our organisation. So it seems natural to me that all these appointments were temporary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked. He is able to identify this as a facsimile signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move through the rest of them pretty quickly as well, please. Could you have a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I actually possibly save time, if I may, because I anticipate that it's going to be the same for each of them. The documents which are tabs 12, 13, 14, and 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 are all these appointments. Rather than having to take him through each and every one of them, could I ask that they all be admitted and marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The relevance of these documents is ... on a thumbnail, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are the appointments of the -- the chiefs of the CSBs and the -- the persons who are going to figure in -- as names in this case. They're all facsimile signatures. The witness went through them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can we consider this during the break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we'd return to this at the -- in a half-hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, we can perhaps deal with the matter you asked us to address you on at the end of lasts week, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- outstanding motion on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We may have to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand -- Mr. O'Sullivan was kind enough to notify me that he thinks that the group of documents that I asked if they could go in without me having go through each one of them the link is too tenuous. Your Honours, I mean, Your Honours have ruled that the first one can go in. The rest are the same. So I don't know if Mr. O'Sullivan, on that basis, has any objection to them effectively going in as bulk. The only thing I accept, the only thing he can say about them, is that these are facsimile signatures, not the really signatures of Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The point that, as I understand it, the Prosecution would have wished to make with the document that has been admitted, which we'll call a specimen for these purposes, we aren't clear as to why it's necessary for the bulk to also go in. Because the point would have been made already, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean, the facsimile signature is merely one aspect. The point that we're seeking to make is that from the moment, effectively, the 31st of March onwards, Mr. Stanisic was the minister of the interior, once the split had been decided on. The firs thing he did was make those appointments of the -- the senior leadership, if you like, of the CSBs. And it shows there -- whether they are facsimile by him or not, those are his appointments. And it's literally the first thing that he does, almost. And that's the importance. Because these are all the heads of the CSBs or the Sarajevo -- Mr. Radovic, in fact, is the assistant minister; Mr. Karisik is the commander of the police; Mr. Savic, Trebinje; Tomo Kovac, Ilidza; Malko Koroman, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I appreciate that something would have passed between counsel during the break, but it would be useful for us to hear on the record what the objection of council for the Defence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the objection is correctly stated by Ms. Korner. This witness was not working in the MUP at the 1st of April, 1992. There's no nexus between any of these documents and this witness. So we say they should not and cannot be offered and admitted through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But the utility of the documents as evidence, the position that I understand you to be articulating, Mr. O'Sullivan, would also apply to the one that had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Objection could have been taken to that one and probably should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- we agree, reluctantly, that the documents may be admitted. I'm not sure whether they will be admitted as one basket with some numbers or whatnot. Whatever the practical way - Anna? - of dealing with these is ... Well, how many of these are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are -- the one that Your Honours have already admitted and - one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight - and a further eight. It's tabs 12 through to 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the Registry would assign them individual numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers assigned are therefore Exhibit P1409 through P1418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Njegus, you said earlier this morning that you knew that Mr. Zupljanin was a successful chief of the security -- what it reads "sister" in Banja Luka, but that should be "centre." And it's at line 22 of page 23. In your interview, you described a meeting you attended in 1993 in Banja Luka about the activities of the CSB Banja Luka. At that stage, did you think that Mr. Zupljanin was a successful chief of the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, why not? Now what was that all about? As the entire MUP was better positioned and as conditions were put in place for that, the head office of the MUP stepped up inspections and provided more instructions to the field offices, including Banja Luka. However, in Banja Luka, we realised that we had to go there to pay them a visit in order to discuss our problems with regard to our functioning and some issues that we were not happy with. At this very moment, I can't remember any more details. But I know that we prepared ourselves for a meeting in Banja Luka and that we, from Banja Luka, went to the central office, as it was known. The meeting was held. We launched our criticism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... right, well this is what I -- I'm sorry. This is the point I want to make. Because I appreciate this is 1993, but you said you were successful. And then, you now say, you launched the criticism. What was the criticism that you had of the CSB, and did it relate to events in 1992? And I think that should be the first question: Was the criticism in respect of anything that had happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Most probably the problems related to that period as well, hence our criticism. I can't remember any of the details. I know that such a meeting had been prepared in all the centres including Banja Luka. I know that there was some criticism to be launched at their work. And I know that I spoke in -- in that sense myself, but that doesn't have to change my opinion that I was the - just a minute ago and that I am voicing again - and that is that Mr. Zupljanin was a successful chief. He was the chief of the largest centre and the centre which had most problems, probably had second number of problems to Sarajevo alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And what's your criteria for being a successful chief?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: What is the criteria? If I remember things properly when we went there, we discussed our cooperation with us, them and us, because we realised that we had too much independence in our work, that we failed to report properly, and things like that. And as far as criteria are concerned, those are well-known and all relate to the security situation and the result of the policing activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, I'm sorry. You said twice now, Mr. Zupljanin was a successful chief of CSB. What, in your view, made him a successful chief of the CSB? I hope that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, it's clear. We're talking after a lapse of time. I know that there were no problems in communication with Mr. Zupljanin. We had good communication with him. He respected all of our decisions, he provided us with all the necessary instructions. He gave us orders. Let me talk about my segment of work. And as for the rest, you should talk to other people who were in charge of other segments. Let me tell you what I base my opinion on. I was the head of legal personnel affairs and affairs concerning foreigners, and in that segment, the Banja Luka centre was among the best, if not the best. There's no doubt about that. And, in that sense, I did not have any problems. That part of the work functioned properly. Well, I suppose that you, Madam Prosecutor, are referring to some other operative segments, some other situations and problems, but those things were not within my immediate purview. And that would be my criteria. The analysis of the part of work that I was in charge of and that part of work was functioning properly in Banja Luka. I could do my job properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You -- accepting that qualification, as far as you're concerned, Mr. Zupljanin kept in touch, reported, and respected the headquarter's decisions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I know it's 1993 and it's a long time ago now, but can you tell us in what respect, therefore, when you went to Banja Luka, you were criticising Mr. Zupljanin for what he did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I really can't remember all the details. But we did analyse things at the central MUP office at one of our collegium meetings. We had received a lot of information about dissatisfaction in some lines of work. And, in general term, we decided to go to Banja Luka to hold a meeting, to launch criticism, and to ask for changes to be instituted there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Believe me, I know what you decided to do. I want to know what it was, please, that you had -- what -- about what, sorry, you had received a lot of information with dissatisfactions in lines of work. What lines of work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I can only suppose after such a long time that most of the problems were related to the operative lines of work. Within my purview, there were fewer problems, although I myself had some criticism towards -- but I can't remember the details. I know that the meeting did take place, and I know that all public security stations chiefs were present at that very large meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you've told us that please -- three times -- can I make this absolutely clear, please, Mr. Njegus. I know there was a meeting and I know lots people were there. I am interested in the problems that led to the meeting. Now, what do you mean by "the problems were related to the operative lines of work"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Again, I have to repeat: I don't remember. I can't remember any specific problems after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it have anything to do with investigations that he should have conducted into major killings, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. This is a leading and after at least four or five times that Mr. Njegus said that he cannot remember, it was a long time ago. Now my learned friend Ms. Korner persistently put her case and again and again tried to -- to press this witness. In spite of his very clear answers, he cannot remember and end of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that that objection was quite foreseeable, Ms. Korner. But, nevertheless, I'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, I take the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, please, sir, to concentrate. What is an operative line of work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Operative lines of work in the MUP are as follows: Crime prevention and the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What was it that was leading to criticism in crime prevention, as far as Banja Luka CSB was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. But I have to repeat once again that I don't remember any details. I know that there was some criticism, but I can't remember any of the details thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe we can look at something later. I want then, please, next, to ask you to look at a document which is - just a moment - yes. If I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, document 65 ter 79; tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this document, which, if we look at the bottom in B/C/S, is dated the 11th of April. Is the Autonomous Region of Krajina sending a dispatch apparently to the MUP saying that it was unanimously proposing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go to page 2 in English. Page 2 in English. Yup. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's unanimously proposing that Stojan Zupljanin as the -- the chief of the Banja Luka Security Centre and Stevan Markovic as chief of police affairs -- But, two questions: Firstly, do you know why the Assembly was making this proposal to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't know. It looks strange in view of the fact that Mr. Zupljanin had previously been assigned to this position as we have already seen. Why he was proposed again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Second question is this: Where a municipal assembly or in this case a regional assembly made a proposal for someone to become chief of the SJB or take any position within the MUP, would the proposal by a municipal assembly always be acted on, or was it within the discretion of the minister?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Situations like that occurred rather frequently. Namely, situations where Municipal Crisis Staffs or, as in this case, the Autonomous Region Assembly would be suggesting some personnel change. We would receive such suggestions and then MUP would make its own assessment. It was on a case-to-case basis that we would or would not accept the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And can I take it, although you were working for the MUP by then, did you see this -- had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. As you can see in the right corner of the document, you can see my handwriting, this note to a Dragan; I don't remember who the Dragan was. A note saying that the decision should be drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, under those circumstances, can I ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit P1417. And exhibits admitted on page 39, line 14, should be assigned numbers P1409 through 1416. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can see -- oh, it's gone again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have it back again, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see here at the bottom there of that it says: "Received by" -- and then somebody has typed "Vukovic." Was that somebody called Danilo Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I can't be certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, because I want to ask you to look at, please, a document which is 10371.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's tab 31. It wasn't on our list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I just want to ask you about this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 10371, please; 65 ter number. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the stamp there. Is -- and signature, is that in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. This document is not heralded on their 65 ter list. And the contents of this document should not be explored with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought we'd been through this heaven knows how many times now. I agree it's not on our 65 ter list. All I want to know is why this gentleman was being sent off. And this witness signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The type of objection which Mr. O'Sullivan has raised is one which I thought would have been raised in terms of an earlier document which we indicated we reluctantly admitted where the document was not on the 65 ter list. But nevertheless, in the way that you phrased the question, you were, in effect, putting the entirety of the document into evidence before it was exhibited. As it turns out, the Defence had no objection to it and we admitted it. But it seems that you're heading down that course again. So, as you said, we have walked the path previously as to the manner of dealing with documents which are not on the 65 ter list and which the side, in this case the Prosecution, doesn't intend to exhibit it. But certainly it is not permissible to, in effect, put the document in evidence. The witness can be shown it and then you can ask a question arising from it. That is the well-established path.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, yes, that's fine. Yes, I will certainly -- I'll deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see that document, Mr. Njegus? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Danilo Vukovic an inspector at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you sign an authorisation sending him to coordinate and direct the work of the criminology service within the CSB Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. I signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that on your own authority? In other words, did you take the decision to send him off? Or was that somebody else's decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: My -- I'm clear [Realtime translation read in error "unclear"] about your question, and I know what I should answer. This was not under my authority. Someone else reached this decision, this authorisation. I only signed it. And in this specific case, I think it was Mr. Cedo Kljajic, under-secretary for public security, who reached this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you said you were clear about my question, not you were unclear, which is what's recorded at 47, line 12.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the question was clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know what the problem was which required Mr. Vukovic to be sent to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember our conversations. This is at a period of time when we were already at Jahorina. We were receiving occasional information about problems in certain areas. First of all, the people that were in charge of operative affairs, but in this specific instance, I was next to them. We did receive information that there were security problems in the area of Bijeljina, and that was the reason why Mr. Vukovic was sent there. He wasn't the only one. I think at the same time or around that time, Mr. Andan [phoen] Dragan was also sent, and maybe some other people from the seat of the MUP, to gain insight into the situation, prepare a report, and assist the people there, on the ground, in resolving the problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you remember what those -- those security problems were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details, but I do know there were security issues, issues relating to protection of property and life, and that there was also problems in the Jajan [phoen] area where mostly Muslim population lived. There were also some crimes, problems with crimes, in Bijeljina. And if you allow me, a small comment: I signed something on behalf or for Mr. Stanisic, one thing that proves that Mr. Stanisic, for instance, wasn't consulted in relation to the signature of mine. Namely, I have signed for him because I was authorised to do so but -- by somebody who was under Mr. Stanisic, who had authority to give such authority. And I apologise for this comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
