utterances.text: All right. So what I -- I mean, Mr. Stanisic delegated the authority to sign on his behalf to Mr. Kljajic. And you're saying that clearly Mr. Kljajic must have had the authority from Mr. Stanisic to delegate further?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's exactly what I'm saying with this example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next, can I ask you, in respect of Mr. Malovic, who you mentioned, to have a look, please, at document number -- 65 ter 2685.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as head of personnel, are you familiar with these payroll lists? Some which we can -- we'll see later you signed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. These payroll lists are more or less familiar to me. These were the lists on the basis of which people were receiving their salary for the preceding month. Well, not in this particular case, but in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this was -- it's a list of those who've been working -- well, it's the special platoon within the Serbian MUP Sokolac, and the first name as the commander is that of Dusko Malovic. Is that the Dusko Malovic you were referring to whose unit you later disbanded in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1417, Your Honours -- apologise, 1418.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we now look, please, very briefly at a document, a newspaper which you had a chance to look at yesterday. It's already an exhibit. P29.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 11A, Mr. Pantelic. I'd like to have the photograph, please, zoomed in on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the text underneath there, I think, is the advisor in the MUP BiH Mico Stanisic and function of the minister during his inspection of the members of the Serbian MUP in Sokolac. Are you able to tell us -- sorry, Mr. Njegus, is the gentleman that Mr. Stanisic, who is on the left, is shaking hands with, is that Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that with certainty because judging on this photograph I would say it is someone older than this Malovic person. He doesn't look like Malovic, but I cannot exclude the possibility that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I won't take that any further. Thank you. Now, can I deal, please, with -- generally with appointments that were made. What sort of authority in -- during the period between April 1992 and the end of 1992 did CSB chiefs have to make their own appointments?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not only chiefs of CSBs. The way I remember things throughout that period, the authorisation for taking people in service or appointing them within the service, was transferred by Mr. Stanisic to a number of his employees, the chief of -- chiefs of centres, then the chief of the service -- National Security Service for the people within that branch, and, if I'm not mistaken, the commander of the detachment of special police. These people were authorised by the minister to take someone into service, to appoint them to different posts, or to launch disciplinary measures, if necessary. I believe that documents confirming this transfer of authority also exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to now show you, please, a document which is already an exhibit. 1D00046; tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look, please, at the second page in B/C/S for a moment. Can we bring up the -- the stamp and signature, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to say - and you've had a chance to look this document before - whether that's a facsimile or a genuine signature by Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: This is a facsimile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go back, please, to the first page, both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This says that: Pursuant to the decision to declare an imminent threat of war, there will be a reorganisation of war units for defending the territory. And then in paragraph 6: "I hereby authorise chiefs of CSB and the commander of the police detachment of the ministry (for Sarajevo CSB) to point officers with appropriate qualifications to command posts of established units and to ensure that the principle of subordination and superiority in the command system is upheld." Now, is that one of the decisions that gives authority to chiefs of CSBs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly one of the decisions. Certainly not the only one. With your permission, my last comment related to this very decision. Now that I've refreshed my recollection, we can see here in this item number 1 that organisation should be transferred from peacetime organisation to wartime organisation and then squads, platoons, companies. That never took place, factually, which goes to confirm something I stated a moment ago, namely, that this whole decision was just something on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the -- well, it's the second decision you said was something on -- just on paper. Are you able to say why, given this order, it wasn't put into effect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know why, but it wasn't. Probably it was all right as an idea, but it wasn't implemented. Most of it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can -- do you know -- can you say why -- sorry. How you know that it wasn't implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I know for certain. If we analyse any of these items, let's take the first one, which deals with the transition from peacetime organisation into a wartime structure, and it says that there's the obligation for all organisation units of the MUP on the grounds be transformed into a structure comprising companies, platoons, squads, et cetera; all that never happened. Except for the special unit, but that's special unit. So I know for sure that this first item was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Mico Stanisic gave an order like this, although it was -- it was done with his facsimile signature, would he check to see whether his order was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, is it -- are we entering into the area of speculation or theory? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a legitimate question dealing with course of practice, isn't it, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But then it should be directed to the theoretical or practical aspect but not with this particular issue, because witness said on numerous occasions that it doesn't exist, actually, these kind of organisations. So maybe my learned friend Ms. Korner could ask him --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- whether in accordance with your knowledge in being a police function --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I really don't -- I'm sorry, Mr. Pantelic. If there's a legitimate objection to my question, whether it's leading or not, that's one thing. Trying to ask the witness questions in the middle of examination-in-chief is quite another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Njegus, if Mico Stanisic gave an order like this, what steps did he take, to your knowledge, if any, to ensure that his order was carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. No, it is not a problem for me to answer at all. I asked myself first whether Mr. Stanisic issued such an instruction and whether he passed such a decision, that is, whether he really signed it, which I really don't know. He may have -- or, rather, it may have been his idea and his instruction. As far as I know, it may not have been that way. It is possible that Cedo Kljajic maybe made this decision, together with Karisik or, who knows who, Tomo Kovac. This is June, yeah, it's possible. So both are possible, so I cannot claim with certainty either one or the other. But since the decision was not implemented, at least most of it, it wasn't implemented on the ground, I should have been the secretary, so I would have known if there had been all these meetings. So we cannot speak about control either. Because according to the information that I have, none of this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So from your understanding, from being at the MUP headquarters, it is possible that Mico Stanisic had delegated to Cedo Kljajic the authority to issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, to your knowledge, did either Mico Stanisic or Cedo Kljajic do anything to enforce the provisions of this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, if we consider what happened -- or, rather, did not happen in practice with regard to this decision, there was nothing to control either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I will repeat the question. Did either Cedo Kljajic or Mico Stanisic, whichever one of them actually decided to issue this order, do anything to enforce it? In other words, to go round or to send people round to check that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Not in that sense, according to the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want -- from there I want to move to the topic of the police being used for combat activities and resubordination. During 1992, were there occasions when police officers would go to the front to carry out combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When they were engaged in combat activities, under whose authority would they be acting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes ... the police of the RS during the war, under the Law on the Military, if I'm not mistaken, but possibly also under the Law on Defence, is an integral part of the armed forces from which everything that later happened follows, both formally speaking and in fact. When a police unit of any size would be deployed to carry out a -- a combat operation, it would be part of the armed forces, that is, the army of RS, and would -- it was subordinate to their command, that is, the command of the VRS. And I'm sure that there's a host of documents showing that it did, indeed, function this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When it was going to the combat zone at the front, who was in charge of the police unit? Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: With regard to this segment and this question, allow me one sentence first. Especially in the early days of the war, but later too, the police had a lot of problems with the VRS, especially on the front line. That's why an initiative was made from the MUP of RS, and I know that there are several clear orders or instructions to that effect, people who were in charge of these matters insisted that an officer from the MUP be the person who took our units to the front line. He would report to the command in charge to which the police were naturally subordinate, and they would obey the orders of that command. But we tried, to the amount that we were able to do it, to -- to have a police officer be the commander of any police unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And you said that there was this initiative. Can you say roughly when that initiative happened? Was it 1992 or was it later?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Which initiative are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one you've just told us about that: "... people who were in charge of these matters insisted that an officer from the MUP be the person who took our units to the front line." When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I must be objective and say that it was really in a later period, not really at the very beginning. Because -- well, beginnings are always difficult. This start-up period was certainly marked by problems and by people not really knowing what to do. So this initiative was really characteristic of a later period, 1993, 1994, to the extent possible, yes, in 1992 also, but mostly later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When the police were engaged in combat activities and resubordinated or subordinated, rather, is the proper word, to the military, if, during the course of that period, a police officer committed a criminal offence, who would be responsible for the investigation? The police or the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion and also under the laws and regulations to the extent I know them, the military bodies would be responsible for an investigation. That is, the services of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the event that the police were not engaged in combat activities with the army, would the police still be subordinated to military regulations simply because the army happened to be within the area; or would they, in those circumstances, be dealt with by the police chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: My conclusion would be that it was the same situation as in my previous answer, because it was a military mission. I think that's the most important criterion for deciding how an investigation is to be conducted. If the unit was carrying out a military mission, then I think that military rules apply, because it was not a civilian mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. A slight misunderstanding. I think it must be the way I phrased the question. If we take, for example, an area in which there were military operations being carried on in one part of the municipality but in another part of the municipality there were police officers not involved in direct combat, who the police then be reporting to? The army or the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, here we're talking about something else altogether. This is about the regular activities of the police, regular tasks, civilian tasks; and in that case, the civilian bodies are in charge. That is, non-military bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Supposing - and let's just look at one other aspect - that it came to the -- once a police unit had returned to ordinary duties and it came to the attention of the police that whilst in the military they had -- the police unit had carried out crimes, what was the responsibility, what was the duty of the police at that stage? The superiors of -- of the unit, if you like.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understand. The duty of the police, that is, everybody in the police, would be to act with the military bodies who were directly responsible for launching a investigation, but the police would have -- would have to take part and contribute to the -- to this -- to solving this case, finding the perpetrator, and so on. To my mind, this is the only way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Njegus, you told us just a short while ago that, especially in the early days of the war, the police had a lot of problems with the VRS, especially on the front line. I wasn't quite sure of what you had in mind when you told us this. Could you explain to us what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for this question. It is really pertinent. Here's what I meant. We all know when the VRS was established. It was at some time in late May. And when it was being established and organised, the sheer strength of that organisation clearly shows that they must have had a million problems. And depending on the circumstances and conditions in the individual municipalities, there were also -- there were always efforts on the part of the army to push the police to the first lines because they were organised already. And, thus, protect military units or send them off to more risky spots, more dangerous ones. And that was a source of big problems and misunderstandings and even conflicts with the military, and that's how it stayed until the end of the war. That's why our executives in the MUP tried hard to have some sort of rules enforced. And that's how we came by these rules that I mentioned a short while ago. That's what I meant when I said that we had a lot of problems with the military. So they simply pushed the police to all possible missions such as securing camps, which was later made public, and so on and so forth. Most army people tried to have police go to the more dangerous spots on the front line or do any kind of -- or carry out any kind of missions that were not desirable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. But it leads me to put a related question, namely, a question regarding paramilitary units. And the question would be if you were aware of such paramilitary units also being resubordinated to the army and the army trying to push the paramilitary troops on the hot spots? Do you know if that happened as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no rules. All sorts of things happened. There were no rules. It all depended on the place. When it came to those renegade groups or paramilitary formations, there were a lot of problems with them. And most often the police did have problems with them. The problems that the police had involved them most often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the army wanted the police to go into combat zones, did they have to make a request either to the CSB or to somebody in the minister -- in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to be engaged, nobody volunteered to be engaged, of course. And that applied to the police. Formal requests either oral or written, I don't know if there were any. I don't remember any such requests actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you deal with any requests for the use of police in combat zones?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, it was logical. People did request the assistance of the police. It didn't go through me. There were requests for the engagement of the police on a broken front line where lives had to be saved, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you able to say who at MUP headquarters would deal with such requests? Or were these requests made at a regional level or, indeed, at a local level?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: As far as I know, all three applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. At MUP headquarters, who would have dealt with such requests? You say it wasn't you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, it wasn't me. I would not be afraid to say that I had been, if I was, but I wasn't. But I believe it was Milenko Karisik, most often, since he was in charge of the special unit that started as a special unit and then became a special detachment. And I suppose that it was also the then-under-secretary for public security as well as the chief of the uniformed police administration. I believe that those were the three persons in the MUP headquarters who received such requests and made decisions on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you to look at one document to see if you can assist, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 1581. And it's tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a -- it's a handwritten order, apparently, stamped and signed by Karadzic, dated 1st of July, 1992. And he says: On the basis of his constitutional powers as Supreme Commander, he orders two platoons of special police forces with 60 men to be sent to Nedzarici and put under the military command of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And then the transfer is going to be done via Ilidza, and they should report to Tomo Kovac. Now, do you know anything about this at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I didn't see it before. I didn't have an occasion to see this order. I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you can't assist as to why Karadzic personally would be issuing an order for special -- two platoons of special police to -- to go to Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I really can't answer your question because I am not privy to that information. This is another of those examples that I spoke about in my statement when I said that such and similar situations were also possible. In a factual term, somebody outside of the MUP institution could issue an order for the engagement of the police in various places. And this is just one of the examples to illustrate that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, well, in that case -- and it was the -- here, as Radovan Karadzic says in his -- sorry. As constitutional power as Supreme Commander. So he had power, did he, as Supreme Commander to give such an order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Probably he had that legal and constitutional power because the police force was an integral part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. Well, thank you. I don't think I can take that document any further. Could you please have a look, now, at document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 33, and it is 65 ter 3129.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is a list of employees for July of 1992. It says minister of the interior, does it, headquarters? Or does that say -- it says "collegium," doesn't it, if we look at the original? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. It says collegium MUP, memorandum, headquarters, collegium, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And does that show a list of the people, including yourself at number 9, who were part of the -- the MUP headquarters, really, the collegium?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes. Nine of us, including myself, represented the MUP collegium in July, as can you see here, and there were five persons who constituted the administrative and technical staff, as can you also see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page in each document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the second page?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that part of your duties, to deal with the -- the salaries of those who worked at -- at senior positions in the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Well, somebody had to draw lists and sign them by way of issuing a -- payment orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm just -- it wasn't intended in any way as a criticism. Just asking, Mr. Njegus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal together as a topic, please, with the various big meetings that you attended. First of all, the 11th of July meeting at tab 35; P -- what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 160. If we go, please, in the second page in both the English and B/C/S, there's a long paragraph about who was at the meeting, and I think your name appears about five sentences -- five, yeah, sentences down. Lines down, sorry. Radomir Njegus acting for legal, administrative, and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you actually spoke at this meeting, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, in the English to page 18; and in the B/C/S. You say -- it's a deeply unhelpful -- to -- you give the -- the -- the ERN number at the top is 0324-1866 and page 16, but I don't think it, unfortunately, that runs properly. Yep, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, is that a record -- you've had a chance to look through these minutes, both at interview and yesterday, didn't you, Mr. Njegus?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And I think you agree that -- obviously they're not verbatim record, but as a summary they're accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Probably. I accept everything that is stated herein, and I would say that in 90 per cent of the cases that was, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're recorded as proposing that a report be compiled on the problems that the MUP was facing with regard to the illegal acts of paramilitary formations. Are you able to assist on what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Of course that after 18 years I can't remember everything. However, in very brief outlines, I would say that I remember that meeting and some others which were held under Mr. Stanisic. I remember about this specific meeting in Belgrade that all centre chiefs attended; and according to the prevalent practice of all police institutions, it was customary and it was normal at those meetings for field officials to present and discuss problems that they faced in the field. Every time Mr. Stanisic gave everybody an opportunity to talk about that. Mr. Zupljanin also discussed his own problems, those that he faced in his area. I'm speaking from memory. And then when he received all that information and when I received all that information, when I heard about all the problems that faced the police officers, I was motivated to do what I said should be done, that a summary should be drafted, and that -- that the authorities, including the president of the Republic and others, should be informed about all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So what you're saying is when you said that when you proposed that a report be compiled on the problems we're facing with regard to illegal acts of paramilitaries, that was on the basis of the information that you had heard from Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Bjelosevic, Mr. Cvijetic, Mr. Savic, and the like?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know if any such report was compiled by anyone in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I don't know anything about paramilitary formations. And as for the summary, I know that it was drafted. And as far as I know, it was dispatched both to the president of the Republic and the president of the government. And I'm talking about the summary of what was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- sorry. I understand that -- you mean, in fact, this document here that we're looking? But was any report done on the problems facing the MUP because of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me, I don't think it was, but I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was it your responsibility to do such a report, as you had made the suggestion; or was it somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: It was not my responsibility. Somebody else should have done it, somebody who was in charge of such problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: People in charge of the uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And at MUP headquarters, that would have been who? Mr. Kljajic or ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kljajic, of course, as the under-secretary for public security; and Mr. Vaso Kusmuk who was at the time chief of administration for uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could we pick this up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I -- yes. Your Honours are rising early today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one -- Your Honours, just 30 seconds. I want to put on the record this practice of this moment with regard to the line of questioning of Ms. Korner. I kindly ask the witness to take off his headphones because I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I think the witness -- if Mr. Pantelic wants to raise something in respect of questioning of the evidence of this witness, then he ought to leave court. He can actually hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, I want to raise the issue about your practice, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... about practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we will pick this up tomorrow morning. And the convenient course would then be to deal with this before the witness is escorted back to the stand. Mr. Njegus, although you are a lawyer, I'm nevertheless obliged to remind you that, having been sworn as a witness, that you cannot speak to any -- to the counsel from either side while you -- until you're released. And in terms of such conversations as you have outside of the court, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we are about to take the adjournment for today, and we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon in this courtroom. Thank you.
